lesson.title: Why Molecules Aren't Flat: The Logic of Electron Repulsion
lesson.summary: VSEPR theory predicts a molecule's three dimensional shape by treating every electron pair around a central atom as a region that repels every other region, pushing them as far apart as geometry allows.
lesson.body:
Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, almost always shortened to VSEPR, rests on one simple physical idea: electrons are negatively charged, and negative charges repel each other. In a molecule, the pairs of valence electrons surrounding a central atom, whether they are shared in a bond or sitting alone as a lone pair, behave like regions of negative charge that push away from one another. To minimize that repulsion, these electron domains spread out as far apart in three dimensional space as they possibly can. The resulting arrangement is not random. It follows predictable geometric patterns that chemists can name and sketch before ever seeing the molecule in a lab.

VSEPR cannot be applied without first drawing a correct Lewis structure, which is why the two concepts are inseparable. The Lewis structure tells you which atom is central, how many bonding pairs connect it to surrounding atoms, and how many lone pairs remain on the central atom without being shared. Every one of those bonding pairs and lone pairs counts as one electron domain, and the total number of domains, called the steric number, is the single most important input to VSEPR. Miscount the lone pairs in the Lewis structure and the predicted shape will be wrong, no matter how carefully the repulsion logic is applied afterward.

Bonding pairs and lone pairs are not treated identically, and understanding why sets up much of the fine detail in later shape predictions. A bonding pair is attracted to two nuclei at once, the central atom and the atom it is bonded to, which pulls the electron cloud into a relatively narrow, disciplined region of space between them. A lone pair, by contrast, is attracted to only one nucleus, so its electron cloud spreads out more broadly and occupies a wider angular space near the central atom. Because lone pairs take up more room, they repel neighboring domains more strongly than bonding pairs do. This difference is what eventually causes measured bond angles to shrink below the idealized values VSEPR predicts for a perfectly symmetric case.

Ammonia, NH3, is a useful first example of the whole process. Drawing its Lewis structure places nitrogen in the center, bonded to three hydrogen atoms with three bonding pairs, and with one lone pair remaining on nitrogen since nitrogen contributes five valence electrons and only three are used in bonds. That gives a steric number of four: three bonding pairs plus one lone pair. VSEPR says these four domains will spread out to minimize repulsion, adopting a tetrahedral arrangement, the geometry that places four regions as far apart as possible around a central point. Everything that follows about the shape of ammonia, and about countless other molecules, starts from this same domain counting exercise applied to a correct Lewis structure.

What makes VSEPR remarkably useful in an introductory course is that it requires no advanced quantum mechanics or orbital math to apply. It is fundamentally an electrostatic argument, negative regions pushing away from other negative regions, yet it correctly predicts the measured three dimensional shapes of an enormous range of main group molecules. Chemists rely on it as a fast, reliable first pass before turning to more detailed bonding models, and it forms the direct foundation for the electron geometry and molecular geometry classifications that come next.
